title: Viking's the Bare Bones Series Program review
summary: NH reviews the Bare Bones Series (bodybuilding.com, by the author of the Gladiator program), which comes as a 3-day full body, a 4-day upper/lower and a 5-day upper/lower + push/pull/legs, all built on rep-goal progression. He likes the exercise selection, superset pairings and autoregulation, but criticises excess volume and isolation work, back squat and deadlift on the same day, and the deadlift/Romanian deadlift rotation. He ranks full body first, ULPPL second, upper/lower third.
claims: He ranks program sources by quality: bodybuilding.com above Reddit, Reddit above T-Nation
Giving a program a cool name is good marketing because it catches the eye of unsuspecting novices
Novice programs should leave a bit of room for autoregulation so trainees can experiment and make their first mistakes; it builds the ability to program for yourself later
A fully idiot-proof program leaves less room for mistakes but also less room for creativity and learning to program
He prefers rep-goal progression to static rep ranges because it adds flexibility and helps progression
A weakness of rep goals is that as you approach the goal the reps can become too easy; he prefers RIR because it gives clearer brackets between and within sets
Three full-body sessions a week is optimal for full body; he likes 3 days plus an arm day
Open a full body day with the back squat because it needs the most thoracic extension and freshness
Doing barbell rows after squats and bench costs a re-warm-up, but the rest lets the lower back recover so you row with a solid lumbar spine; a price worth paying
A rep goal of 25 total reps over 3 sets forces about 7-8 reps per set, high enough to prevent ego lifting and stay safe
A 32-rep goal on the squat demands stamina and form maintenance that many novices lack
Supersetting accessories (e.g. leg curls with seated DB press, pulldowns with abs/calves) saves time and can finish the session with a giant set
Opening a day with deadlifts for 2 sets totalling 12 reps keeps volume high but intensity relevant; it shows the author knows what he is doing
Deadlift and Romanian deadlift do not work as a rotation: RDL at ~10 reps per set is not strength work, so they serve different purposes
He favours deadlifting once every 8 days, but once every 14 days is too infrequent
He dislikes the leg press; many people get lower back pain from it
Full body programs often slap an exercise in for a body part just to justify the label; in practice they are an upper/lower modulation of volume
Training the same back squat and bench at full volume twice a week risks overuse injuries; use a variation (close-grip bench, pause squat) on the second day instead
You can bench and squat twice a week without repeating the same lift: variations stay specific, carry over and may progress better over time
Programs need a dedicated static hip hinge such as the Romanian deadlift; leg curls do not make up for missing hip hinges
Replace barbell rows with dumbbell or seal rows on the RDL day to spare the lower back
Days with too many exercises are wasted once you run out of juice; you stop really training
Horizontal press, horizontal row and vertical press is the winning combo for an upper day
Adding more and more exercises lowers intensity on the top strength work because you subconsciously save energy, which hurts progression
Fewer exercises gives more quality tonnage, less time in the gym and less junk volume
Never back squat and then deadlift heavy on the same day, especially as main lifts: the second lift suffers and injury risk rises
Get as much as possible from as little work as possible; training more forces you to keep expanding the program until sessions take 2-2.5 hours
In the hierarchy of vertical pulls, pull-ups beat machines and weighted pull-ups beat pull-ups; prioritise them
Romanian deadlifts can be done twice a week because they are not too taxing if you know how to do them
Squat and deadlift variations plus a smidgen of isolation is enough to build massive legs
Minimalism works for novices and intermediates; don't do every isolation movement, but don't neglect muscle groups either
When rest days are scarce (5-day ULPPL with one rest day between cycles) each session must be minimal
For 3 sets with a 25-rep goal when already tired he would prefer a 35-rep goal to make it manageable
An exercise that isn't fatiguing isn't taxing and isn't giving gains, so cut it (straight-arm pulldowns)
A variation of the squat has more carryover than adding hack squats afterwards
Barbell rows fit as a strength lift, work as a hip hinge and carry over to the deadlift
The long head of the triceps recovers fast, so overhead extensions can go on the leg day
Split templates like PPL are shackled by rules they don't want to follow; this is why he prefers gentleman splits
Verdict: good program, but the creator makes you do too much, has rotation issues and too much isolation; an anti-minimalist mindset backfires for novices and intermediates
